extracted.intended_audience: scholars and students of journalism, mass communication, and sociology; researchers interested in news production and organizational studies
extracted.subtask_description: Analyzing how newspapers and television newsrooms select, construct, and present events as news — i.e., the criteria and organizational processes that make occurrences publicly discussable. Draws on participant observation to theorize news as a socially constructed frame, an institution, and a professionally routinized practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: News as Frame
rubrics_metrics.description: News functions as a window on the world: through its frame Americans learn about themselves, institutions, leaders, life styles, and other nations; the view depends on the characteristics of the frame (size, panes, clarity) and the vantage point of the viewer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the window metaphor to evaluate how selection, framing, and vantage (organizational placement, professional perspective) determine which aspects of reality are visible to audiences. Consider whether the organization’s structure and routines constrict or enlarge the frame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness — mutual pertinence to speaker/listener
rubrics_metrics.description: Items must be judged pertinent to both speaker and listener to qualify as newsworthy and must somehow present themselves to the speaker in the course of events (e.g., the professor’s choice to tell her spouse about Joe’s remark rather than about three green lights).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a detail/event is selected because it will be meaningful to the intended audience; examine negotiation between producer and audience expectations when assessing newsworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility — spatial and temporal purview
rubrics_metrics.description: Particulars embedded in strips of ongoing activity become reportable only if they enter the reporter’s spatial and temporal purview (i.e., are within reach to be observed or learned about).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess selections by asking how and when information became available to the reporter (beat access, presence at scene, timing). Field-site differences (local TV vs. city desk vs. press room) alter what can come into view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stratification and access to knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Some items are not related because knowledge is embedded in stratification systems — those with more power may hold conversations or information inaccessible to lower-status reporters (example: president and provost discussing firings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine how organizational hierarchies, social status, and institutional gatekeeping restrict reporters’ access to certain facts and thereby shape coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taken-for-granted/tacit professional knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Some particulars are omitted from reports because they are taken for granted as routine occupational skills or background (e.g., placement of a chair at a departmental meeting; what counts as a legitimate meeting detail).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating omission or inclusion, consider what insiders treat as routine knowledge and therefore do not report; probe tacit assumptions that render certain facts invisible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Noticing and professional perspective (attention)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some items are not noticed because of newsworkers’ perspectives or professional incapacity; what journalists attend to is shaped by training, routines, and occupational concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how journalists’ training, beats, and perspectives channel attention; compare what different reporters notice or ignore as an indicator of professional filter effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professionalism and organizational needs (routinization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Newswork is routinized: professionalism developed in conjunction with modern news organizations, and professional practices serve organizational needs; these routines both enable production and help legitimate the status quo even as occasional conflicts with management arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate news production by identifying organizational routines (assignment, deadlines, program lengths) and asking how professional norms accommodate or reproduce those needs and organizational interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: News as an institution — circulation and shaping of knowledge / agenda-setting
rubrics_metrics.description: News is an institutional method of making information available to consumers and an ally of legitimated institutions; topics given most coverage in the media are likely to become seen by audiences as the most pressing (agenda-setting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure coverage frequency, placement, and prominence to evaluate agenda-setting effects; consider how institutional ties (official sources, floated ideas) amplify certain topics and priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on legitimated/official sources
rubrics_metrics.description: News routinely uses legitimated institutions and sources (e.g., anonymous ‘reliable source’ floats) — news is an ally of legitimated institutions and officials can use media channels strategically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess sourcing patterns (official vs. grassroots) and note how privileging legitimated sources shapes the scope and framing of stories and can serve institutional interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative construction and the news lead
rubrics_metrics.description: The news lead proclaims that what follows is factual and veridical; selection of a lead and narrative opening frames the event as a hard-nosed factual account rather than myth or fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how opening sentences and story structure frame an event’s character (factual, sensational, trivial); compare lead choice to alternative framings to reveal construction decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making news as a negotiated enterprise
rubrics_metrics.description: Making news is negotiated — between speakers and listeners in ordinary conversation and among reporters, editors, managers, and institutional actors — so selection and presentation emerge from interaction and bargaining.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace decision-making chains (assignment meetings, editorial debates) to reveal negotiation dynamics and who exercises influence over what becomes news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation — transformation of happenings into publicly discussable events
rubrics_metrics.description: News imparts a public character to occurrences, transforming mere happenings into events that can be publicly discussed, debated, and remembered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether and how a report turns an occurrence into a public event (contextualization, attribution, narrative closure) and what social meaning it assigns to that occurrence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative influence of entertainment media versus news
rubrics_metrics.description: News is not the only mass medium shaping public understanding; entertainment television and other media can influence attitudes and images (e.g., TV depictions of groups or characters shaping viewers’ beliefs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating the news’s social effects, situate it among other media influences; do not assume news alone explains public attitudes — measure entertainment exposure and content as comparative factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsroom composition and structural bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Workforce composition (gender, status) and newsroom practices affect coverage and staff retention (example: a woman reporter resigned claiming sexism), which in turn influence which topics receive attention and how they are framed (e.g., coverage of the women’s movement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate demographic and institutional diversity within newsrooms and consider how unequal representation or workplace culture skews beats, sourcing, and interpretive frames.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims of objectivity as strategic ritual
rubrics_metrics.description: Although news presents itself as objective and factual, it is socially constructed; claims to objectivity operate as strategic rituals that legitimate reporting practices and organizational authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinize rituals of objectivity (use of passive voice, anonymous sourcing, balancing devices) to see how they are employed to legitimate certain constructions while masking selection decisions.
